strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP problem: converting naturally occurring conversational feedback into preference training data. The resulting 20,281-example dataset offers a useful direction for learning from real interactions and retaining multi-turn context.

The experiments provide substantial evidence of improved automatic benchmark performance across three model families. For example, Phi-3 trained on WF GPT-4 improves AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate from 24.3% to 34.9% and Arena-Hard win rate from 15.4% to 32.4% (Table 3). These external benchmarks support utility beyond the proposed checklist evaluation.

The experimental design includes expert-generated and on-policy data, regenerated UltraFeedback baselines, and evaluation with and without checklists. The stated separation of training and test conversations and users is a valuable precaution.

The appendices provide rubrics, annotation procedures, prompts, and principal training hyperparameters. Human validation covers 50 conversations for feedback identification and 200 for checklist evaluation; DSAT precision of 83.3% provides useful support for feedback mining. The limitations acknowledge selection bias and potentially harmful preferences.
weaknesses: The central claim of better alignment with actual user preferences needs stronger independent validation. GPT-4 produces preference summaries, expert responses, filtering decisions, and checklist judgments, creating substantial scope for shared model biases. The human study assesses judgments against supplied checklists without establishing that those summaries faithfully represent the original feedback or reporting human preference gains for the trained models. GPT–human checklist agreement is only 57.14%, with κ = 0.372 (Table 7). An audit against original feedback and a human comparison of model outputs would strengthen this claim.

The contribution of feedback itself is not isolated. WildFeedback and UltraFeedback differ in prompt distribution, context length, and preference-pair construction. In particular, expert WildFeedback contrasts newly generated responses against historical responses that triggered dissatisfaction, while the UltraFeedback baseline compares newly generated responses. A matched WildChat baseline without feedback conditioning would clarify whether feedback adds value beyond domain adaptation and response regeneration; SFT-only results would also clarify the benefit of preference-pair training.

The custom test set limits the generality of the conclusions. Selecting ten examples with the most mutually similar preferences within each of 70 clusters explicitly favors common preferences, but does not establish that the resulting 540 examples represent the population majority. Combined with feedback-based selection and DSAT recall of 48.4%, this leaves substantial uncertainty about coverage. Claims about diverse and evolving user preferences require broader or longitudinal evidence.

Claims of significant and consistent superiority are stronger than the reported results. Qwen-2 WF GPT-4 underperforms UF GPT-4 on AlpacaEval length-controlled win rate, 39.4% versus 40.6%, and MT-Bench, 7.60 versus 7.66 (Table 3). Several other margins are small, and confidence intervals, significance tests, and training-seed variability are not reported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the useful appendix. The dataset is described only as becoming available soon, and the submission does not supply released artifacts or sufficient details to reconstruct the exact splits and curation, including clustering embeddings, deduplication thresholds, generation settings, and the hyperparameter-selection protocol. Together with the unresolved preference-validation and attribution questions, this leaves the Findings recommendation borderline rather than clearly positive.
